1.pericope_label: Moreover the word of the Lord came to me, saying, Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying, Thus saith the Lord; I remember thee, the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown. Israel was holiness unto the Lord, and the firstfruits of his increase: all that devour him shall offend; evil shall come upon them, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch judge the six long discourses to be treatises compiled in writing out of the prophet's oral preaching, since they carry none of the dates and circumstances the later sayings carry; Ellicott derives them instead from the book's own history, as a precis of the roll burnt by the king and rewritten from memory, and reads the marriage figure back through the earlier prophets and forward to the later.

Gill takes the opening as the general title of the whole book and lists what made Israel holiness to the Lord, down to the words on the front of the high priest's mitre; Calvin takes the remembered kindness to be God's own rather than theirs, and refuses to let the title of firstfruits stand as praise, since it is set in implied contrast with the wickedness that followed.

Clarke dates the youth to the coming out of Egypt and the espousals to the receiving of the law, insists the kindness was God's and not theirs, and turns devouring Israel into a trespass on divine property; Wesley makes the remembered kindness mutual, a reminder of what was between them.

Henry makes the sending a lesson for ministers, who should take out a fresh commission by faith and prayer and be able to say not merely that the Lord sent them but that he sent them to speak this, and marks the move from a pleasant retirement into a noisy city.

debates.question: What are these opening chapters?

positions.position: The beginning of the book proper and the prophet's first sermon, the preceding chapter being only a preface.
Treatises compiled in writing out of oral addresses, not discourses delivered before the people.
A precis of the roll destroyed by the king and afterwards rewritten from memory, with some additions and possibly omissions.

debates.question: Whose kindness is remembered?

positions.position: God's own, shown in taking them to be his people, and not theirs to him.
Israel's: the faithfulness of the past set against the unfaithfulness of the present.
Mutual, a reminder of the kindness that was between them.

debates.question: What does it mean that Israel was holiness to the Lord?

positions.position: Choice, covenant, holy laws, a sanctuary among them, and a high priest wearing the words on his mitre.
A priestly character in the nation itself, consecrated as firstfruits of the harvest of the world.
As wholly the Lord's as the firstfruits were the priests' own property.
Not praise at all, but a title standing in implied contrast with the wickedness that followed.

outliers.claim: Turns the particular commission into a rule for ministers: let a man compare what he has to deliver with the word, so as to say not only that the Lord sent him but that he sent him to speak this.

Traces the verb for offending through the ceremonial law and prefers to render it shall be condemned or shall be made to suffer, the devourers being guilty as of a sacrilege that will not go unpunished.

themes: Moreover the word of the Lord came to me, saying,

Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying, Thus saith the Lord; I remember thee, the kindness of thy youth, the love of thine espousals, when thou wentest after me in the wilderness, in a land that was not sown.
Israel was holiness unto the Lord, and the firstfruits of his increase: all that devour him shall offend; evil shall come upon them, saith the Lord.

4.pericope_label: Hear ye the word of the Lord, O house of Jacob, and all the families of the house of Israel: Thus saith the Lord, What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me, and have walked after vanity, and are become vain? Neither said they, Where is the Lord that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, that led us through the wilderness, through a land of deserts and of pits, through a land of drought, and of the shadow of death, through a land that no man passed through, and where no man dwelt? And I brought you into a plentiful country, to eat the fruit thereof and the goodness thereof; but when ye entered, ye defiled my land, and made mine heritage an abomination. The priests said not, Where is the Lord? and they that handle the law knew me not: the pastors also transgressed against me, and the prophets prophesied by Baal, and walked after things that do not profit.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch let the summons run against the whole people, keep the benefits of the exodus in view, explain why the land is called a heritage, and render the plentiful country as fruitful fields against the wilderness just described; Ellicott alone qualifies the picture of the desert as true of part but not the whole of the region, notes that the Greek took the word for a proper name, dates the degeneracy to the settlement, and separates the priestly law-handlers from the later order of scribes.

Gill limits the summons to the two tribes and their families and denies the premise of the question, since there is no unrighteousness in God nor any failure of his promises; Calvin reads the preface as a bid for attention, finds two crimes rather than one, and turns the passage against those who plead that they only followed their rulers.

Clarke asks whether anything cruel or tyrannical was ever found in the law or the government, describes a desert where no family could have subsisted, and reads the pastors as kings and civil rulers and the law-handlers as expositors of its spiritual meaning.

debates.question: Who is summoned to hear?

positions.position: The two remaining tribes and their families, the ten having long since gone into captivity.
The whole people.

debates.question: Who were those that handled the law?

positions.position: Expositors, whose office was to draw out the law's spiritual meaning.
Priests, since the order of non-priestly scribes does not appear until after the captivity.

debates.question: How is the picture of the wilderness to be taken?

positions.position: Literally and at full strength: no family could have subsisted there, much less six hundred thousand men.
As colours laid on to heighten a contrast, true of part but not of the whole region.
As the record of benefits they took no thought of, though they owed him everything.

outliers.claim: Answers in advance the plea that the common people lacked learning to tell light from darkness and only followed their rulers: the prophet does not cast their faults on the leaders, and from the least to the greatest they had rejected God and his law.
Observes that what weighed most on the prophets was that those called to guide the people were the chief agents in the evil, and that this rebuke came from the lips of a priest.

themes: Hear ye the word of the Lord, O house of Jacob, and all the families of the house of Israel:
Thus saith the Lord, What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me, and have walked after vanity, and are become vain?

Neither said they, Where is the Lord that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, that led us through the wilderness, through a land of deserts and of pits, through a land of drought, and of the shadow of death, through a land that no man passed through, and where no man dwelt?
And I brought you into a plentiful country, to eat the fruit thereof and the goodness thereof; but when ye entered, ye defiled my land, and made mine heritage an abomination.

The priests said not, Where is the Lord? and they that handle the law knew me not: the pastors also transgressed against me, and the prophets prophesied by Baal, and walked after things that do not profit.

9.pericope_label: Wherefore I will yet plead with you, saith the Lord, and with your children’s children will I plead. For pass over the isles of Chittim, and see; and send unto Kedar, and consider diligently, and see if there be such a thing. Hath a nation changed their gods, which are yet no gods? but my people have changed their glory for that which doth not profit. Be astonished, O ye heavens, at this, and be horribly afraid, be ye very desolate, saith the Lord. For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.

schools.summary: Ellicott hears in the pleading the injured husband of an earlier prophet setting out an indictment, takes the two far countries as furthest west and furthest east rather than identifying them, points at the word for nation as emphatically heathen, glosses the verb of astonishment as thunder-stricken, and distinguishes the spring water of the fountain from the surface water of a tank.

Gill derives the western name from a son of Javan and reports the Jewish account of two peoples worshipping water and fire without exchanging gods, and dwells on the aggravation that these were the people of God, who may fall into great sins and yet remain his; Calvin gets from the word yet that God keeps his right entire to their children's children, refuses to let heathen constancy count as praise, and explains why prophets address heaven and earth in hopeless cases.

Clarke keeps the pleading forensic, prefers to place the Chittim in Italy and the European coast against the usual Cyprus, sharpens the comparison with nations that kept gods they owed nothing to, raises the question whether the heavens are commanded or described, and presses broken cisterns to mean vessels ill made and not staunch.
Henry makes the pleading the alternative to punishment, since God pleads before he punishes, and adds that those who deal with sinners must urge a variety of arguments and follow their blow.

debates.question: What does it mean that God will yet plead with them?

positions.position: A legal process maintained to conviction, vindicating his own conduct and proving theirs wicked.
The injured husband appearing as accuser and setting out the bride's guilt as an indictment.
Either words or deeds, reproof or punishment.
The alternative to punishment, since God pleads with sinners before he punishes them.
The assertion of a right not yet exhausted, to be pursued to their children's children.

debates.question: Where is Chittim?

positions.position: Cyprus, the name then extended by the Hebrews to all islands and maritime places.
Italy and the neighbouring European coast, against both Cyprus and Macedonia.
Greece, though the Hebrews thought the term belonged properly to the Macedonians.
Whatever lies furthest west, the pair standing for the whole earth.

debates.question: Are the heavens commanded to be astonished, or described as astonished?

positions.position: The original will admit either.
Commanded, in an adjuration already familiar from the older scriptures.
Addressed as things without understanding, which prophets do in hopeless cases where men will not learn.

outliers.claim: Dwells on whose evils these were: the aggravation is that the people of God committed them, and such may fall into great sins and yet remain his, which he offers not as encouragement to sin but as relief under the sense of it.
Measures the folly of the exchange: to leave an old friend for a new one is base, but where there is no compensation it is folly, levity and madness together.

themes: Wherefore I will yet plead with you, saith the Lord, and with your children’s children will I plead.
For pass over the isles of Chittim, and see; and send unto Kedar, and consider diligently, and see if there be such a thing.
Hath a nation changed their gods, which are yet no gods? but my people have changed their glory for that which doth not profit.
Be astonished, O ye heavens, at this, and be horribly afraid, be ye very desolate, saith the Lord.
For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water.

14.pericope_label: Is Israel a servant? is he a homeborn slave? why is he spoiled? The young lions roared upon him, and yelled, and they made his land waste: his cities are burned without inhabitant. Also the children of Noph and Tahapanes have broken the crown of thy head. Hast thou not procured this unto thyself, in that thou hast forsaken the Lord thy God, when he led thee by the way?

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain the appearance of Egypt from the prophet's own moment, help being sought there against the Chaldeans as it had once been sought against Assyria, and refuse to read the way as the right way of life since the clause fixes the leading within a definite time; Ellicott reverses the opening question by making servant a title of honour, takes the lions literally rather than as symbols of invaders, weighs the two identifications of the first Egyptian city, and renders the verb of breaking as depasturing so as to produce baldness.

Gill takes the servant for one carried captive and used as a slave, makes the lions the kings of Assyria and Babylon on the Jewish commentators' authority, identifies the two cities, and lays the whole desolation to their own idolatry; Calvin argues from their charter that they were free beyond all nations as the firstborn son, adds contempt to cruelty in the figure of the beasts, reads the particle as bringing their own friends against them, and makes the evil a thing they concocted and must swallow.

Clarke asks whether the man is a slave bought with money or a servant born in the house and answers, a son; he names the Assyrians as the lions, gives the two cities their Greek names, and supplies a date for the broken crown in the defeat and death of the good king.

Henry piles up the reasons for denying the servitude: they are children and heirs, the seed of God's friend and of his chosen, not the son of the bondwoman but of the free, designed for dominion and not for servitude.

debates.question: What does the question about a servant mean?

positions.position: A denial: he is a son, not a slave bought with money nor a servant born in the house.
A description of the state he has fallen into, carried captive and used as a slave.
An affirmation reversed: servant is a title of honour, and the question is why the household servant of Jehovah is treated as one with no master to protect him.

debates.question: Are the lions figurative or literal?

positions.position: Figurative, of the kings of the nations, likened to lions for strength and cruelty.
Figurative, and with contempt added to cruelty, since it is more degrading to be torn by beasts.
Literal: lions had attacked and made the land waste, not merely as symbols of invaders.

debates.question: What way was it that he led them in?

positions.position: The particular road he brought them by, since the clause fixes the leading within a definite time while God leads rightly at all times.
Scarcely the literal path through the wilderness, but rather the true way of life.

outliers.claim: Declines the suggestion that the shame lies in being beaten by a people the old historians called unwarlike, whose men were said to keep to the occupations of women, since Scripture does not say it.
Supplies a date for the broken crown of the head: the defeat and death of the good king in battle with the Egyptians.

themes: Is Israel a servant? is he a homeborn slave? why is he spoiled?
The young lions roared upon him, and yelled, and they made his land waste: his cities are burned without inhabitant.
Also the children of Noph and Tahapanes have broken the crown of thy head.
Hast thou not procured this unto thyself, in that thou hast forsaken the Lord thy God, when he led thee by the way?

18.pericope_label: And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Sihor? or what hast thou to do in the way of Assyria, to drink the waters of the river? Thine own wickedness shall correct thee, and thy backslidings shall reprove thee: know therefore and see that it is an evil thing and bitter, that thou hast forsaken the Lord thy God, and that my fear is not in thee, saith the Lord God of hosts.

schools.summary: Ellicott states the principle that great rivers were in the poetry of the prophets the natural symbols of the kingdoms they flowed through, glosses the first name as the turbid water and notes that elsewhere it means the border stream, shows the alliance policy was old by naming the kings who had tried it, and reads the rising strain as the eternal law of retribution.

Gill allows either an imitation of Egyptian idols or the sending of ambassadors, gives two historical instances of the second, and offers two constructions of the correcting wickedness; Calvin makes the two errands an image of aggravated sin, comparing a sick man who passes by his cure for expedients that injure him, and holds that the judgment would be plain in their very sins even if God were silent.

Clarke identifies the two rivers and calls the allies a broken reed and a leaky cistern, two nations always jealous of Israel and seeking its ruin; Wesley keeps the plain sense that their own wickedness is the cause of their correction, and that they need only consider to be convinced.

debates.question: How does their own wickedness correct them?

positions.position: By the ill success of the errands, which was itself an instruction, or else as the just reason why the Lord chastened them.
As the cause of the correction God sends.
As retribution intrinsic to the act, our pleasant vices becoming whips to scourge us.
As a judgment plain in the sins themselves, even if God were silent and there were no accuser at all.

debates.question: What was wrong with the two alliances?

positions.position: They were made with nations always jealous of Israel and seeking its ruin, a broken reed and a leaky cistern.
They were sought when God was near, and against an express word.
They were vain remedies chosen instead of the one remedy of reconciliation, and so heaped up new causes of misery.
They were an old and repeatedly rebuked policy of courting now one great kingdom and now the other.

outliers.claim: Compares them to a sick man who knows the cause of his disease and, passing by what would cure him, has recourse to expedients that injure his recovery, and asks whether such a man is not held worthy to die.
Shows the alliance policy was no new one, naming the kings who had courted Assyria, Babylon and Egypt in turn, and the earlier prophet who had rebuked both courses.

themes: And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Sihor? or what hast thou to do in the way of Assyria, to drink the waters of the river?

Thine own wickedness shall correct thee, and thy backslidings shall reprove thee: know therefore and see that it is an evil thing and bitter, that thou hast forsaken the Lord thy God, and that my fear is not in thee, saith the Lord God of hosts.

20.pericope_label: For of old time I have broken thy yoke, and burst thy bands; and thou saidst, I will not transgress; when upon every high hill and under every green tree thou wanderest, playing the harlot. Yet I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed: how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch correct the figure of the vine against the older song of the vineyard, where Israel was the vineyard and here is the vine itself, and press the word for what it became to mean degenerate suckers rather than shoots; Ellicott prefers the second person in the opening clause and the reading I will not serve in the next, identifies the localities and the fascination of tree-worship, gives the vine its Hebrew name and the valley behind it, and marks how the stress differs from the older song.

Gill keeps the received reading in which God breaks the yoke the nations had laid on them, and takes the noble vine of the fathers who had the right seed of grace in them; Calvin agrees on the reading of the second clause but rejects the gloss everyone had built on it, and asks why a vine at all, answering that God calls his Church his vine rather than his pasture because vines are the most precious property.

Clarke reports the critics who put the verbs in the second person and escapes by way of the Aramaic paraphrase, notes the worshippers' plea that elevation assisted devotion, and reads the vine of privileges given and a life reasonably expected in return; Wesley keeps the deliverance from Egyptian bondage, the hidden deity under the shade, and the force of a verb that means hastening from one idol to the next.

Henry takes the wandering itself for the point: they went from one place of worship to another like people unsettled and still unsatisfied, for those who leave God wander endlessly and a vagrant lust is insatiable.

debates.question: Who broke the yoke?

positions.position: God did, breaking the yoke the nations had laid on their necks at the deliverance from Egypt and in the days of the judges.
Israel did, casting off all allegiance and restraint.
The versions differ, and the Aramaic paraphrase removes the difficulty by making God break the yoke of the people from their neck.

debates.question: What did they say when the yoke was broken?

positions.position: I will not serve, the defiance of a nation throwing off its allegiance.
I will not serve, but not, as the prevailing gloss had it, I will not serve idols, which is strained enough to have caused the change of a letter.

debates.question: What is the point of the noble vine?

positions.position: The fathers, who had the right seed of grace in them and deserved imitation by their posterity.
The privileges given, the fullest instruction and purest ordinances, against which the fruit is now bad.
The value God sets on his Church, called his vine rather than his pasture or his field.
The degeneration of what God planted, where the older song stressed evil mingled with good.

outliers.claim: Draws a rule from the wandering: those who leave God wander endlessly, and a vagrant lust is insatiable.
Corrects the figure against the older song of the vineyard: there Israel is the vineyard planted with noble vines, here Israel is the vine itself, planted by Jahveh.

themes: For of old time I have broken thy yoke, and burst thy bands; and thou saidst, I will not transgress; when upon every high hill and under every green tree thou wanderest, playing the harlot.
Yet I had planted thee a noble vine, wholly a right seed: how then art thou turned into the degenerate plant of a strange vine unto me?

22.pericope_label: For though thou wash thee with nitre, and take thee much soap, yet thine iniquity is marked before me, saith the Lord God. How canst thou say, I am not polluted, I have not gone after Baalim? see thy way in the valley, know what thou hast done: thou art a swift dromedary traversing her ways; A wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure; in her occasion who can turn her away? all they that seek her will not weary themselves; in her month they shall find her. Withhold thy foot from being unshod, and thy throat from thirst: but thou saidst, There is no hope: no; for I have loved strangers, and after them will I go.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch keep the wild ass's month to the beast and make it her breeding month, refusing both the new moon as a feast and any monthly period; Ellicott locates the mineral alkali in the Egyptian lakes that gave it its name, corrects the second detergent to the potash of plant ashes, sets the murderer of the stage beside the verse, answers the plea of innocence from the history of the reformation, and calls the wild ass a type of passion that defies control.

Gill confesses the nitre of the ancients is unknown to us and reports the Jewish guesses at it, and offers three constructions of the unshod foot; Calvin hears hypocrites objecting that they are the holy seed, so that the prophets had to drive a hard wedge into a hard knot, makes the wild ass a figure of untamable madness, and observes that what was actually asked was not a journey but that they remain still and quiet.

Clarke insists on natron rather than nitre and explains the proverb about vinegar upon it, describes the fever that makes the beast open mouth and nostrils to the wind, and turns her month into the contrast that carries the comparison, since the animal has a season and these desires none; Wesley alone hears a promise in the same phrase, that a time may come in her afflictions when she grows tamer and willing to receive counsel.

debates.question: What are the two detergents?

positions.position: The nitre of the ancients is unknown to us, and saltpetre is put in its room; the Jewish guesses are alum, a cleansing dust, or an earth used on garments.
Natron, a substance quite different from our nitre, still used in the east for washing.
The mineral alkali of the Egyptian natron lakes, with potash from plant ashes for the second, not soap as we know it.

debates.question: What does in her month mean?

positions.position: The month appointed for the gratification of the beast's natural desire.
The season when the stimulus of animal desire is strongest.
The contrast that carries the comparison: the beast is dangerous only for a season, while these desires were never satiated.
A promise: a time may come in her afflictions when she grows tamer and willing to receive counsel.

debates.question: What is the unshod foot?

positions.position: Long journeys abroad for help, or going naked into captivity, or a euphemism for the adulteress putting off her shoes.
The euphemism, extended to the throat and the libations that only increase the appetite.
The apostate wife rushing barefoot into the streets, or possibly the bare feet of the worship itself, shoes being put off at the temple door.
The poverty these courses will bring, without shoes and without the means to quench thirst.

outliers.claim: Explains the proverb comparing songs sung to a heavy heart with vinegar upon natron: there is no affinity between them, and any attempt to unite them makes strife.
Reports the objection the prophets had to meet, are we not God's holy people, is not this the holy seed, and says a hard wedge had to be driven into a hard knot.

themes: For though thou wash thee with nitre, and take thee much soap, yet thine iniquity is marked before me, saith the Lord God.
How canst thou say, I am not polluted, I have not gone after Baalim? see thy way in the valley, know what thou hast done: thou art a swift dromedary traversing her ways;

A wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure; in her occasion who can turn her away? all they that seek her will not weary themselves; in her month they shall find her.
Withhold thy foot from being unshod, and thy throat from thirst: but thou saidst, There is no hope: no; for I have loved strangers, and after them will I go.

26.pericope_label: As the thief is ashamed when he is found, so is the house of Israel ashamed; they, their kings, their princes, and their priests, and their prophets, Saying to a stock, Thou art my father; and to a stone, Thou hast brought me forth: for they have turned their back unto me, and not their face: but in the time of their trouble they will say, Arise, and save us. But where are thy gods that thou hast made thee? let them arise, if they can save thee in the time of thy trouble: for according to the number of thy cities are thy gods, O Judah.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the shame as already felt and therefore as opening a possibility of repentance, explains from the feminine gender of the second noun why the stone is made the mother, hears the sentences as a quotation from the idolatrous hymns, and follows the turned back to the outstretched hands of the time of trouble.

Gill adds the qualification the figure of the thief needs, that it is the man reckoned honest who is ashamed at being found out, and has the Lord answering his own question about the gods they made themselves; Calvin drains the remorse out of the shame, making it exposure rather than repentance, and isolates as the detestable thing not the bending of the knee but the seeking of salvation from a statue.

Clarke puts the thief's shame in the future, when God arrests them in their idolatries, marks what is claimed when a man calls a tree his father, and observes that the tutelary deity of every heathen city has only been refined into the tutelary saint of every Christian one; Wesley calls it sottish stupidity, notes that they turn their faces towards their idols, and invites them to try whether any of their gods or all together can help.

debates.question: How is the thief's shame to be taken?

positions.position: As future: they shall be confounded when God arrests them in their idolatries.
As already felt, and so as evidence that conscience is roused and repentance possible.
As present, but of exposure rather than remorse: the impiety was as public as a thief taken in the act.
As belonging only to one reckoned honest, since those notorious for theft feel nothing when caught.

debates.question: What is worst in saying to a stock, Thou art my father?

positions.position: That to produce and sustain a being is the property of the true God alone.
That a lifeless stock or stone is taken for one's maker.
Not the outward act of bending the knee, but the seeking of salvation from the statue.
That the words read like an actual quotation from the hymns of the ritual.

outliers.claim: Explains the figurative parentage from the grammar: the word for stone is feminine in Hebrew, and so the parts of father and mother are assigned by the language itself.

Observes that the tutelary deity every heathen city had has only been refined into the tutelary saint every Christian city has, with a procession and worship peculiar to himself, so that not much of the old idolatry is lost.

themes: As the thief is ashamed when he is found, so is the house of Israel ashamed; they, their kings, their princes, and their priests, and their prophets,

Saying to a stock, Thou art my father; and to a stone, Thou hast brought me forth: for they have turned their back unto me, and not their face: but in the time of their trouble they will say, Arise, and save us.
But where are thy gods that thou hast made thee? let them arise, if they can save thee in the time of thy trouble: for according to the number of thy cities are thy gods, O Judah.

29.pericope_label: Wherefore will ye plead with me? ye all have transgressed against me, saith the Lord. In vain have I smitten your children; they received no correction: your own sword hath devoured your prophets, like a destroying lion. O generation, see ye the word of the Lord. Have I been a wilderness unto Israel? a land of darkness? wherefore say my people, We are lords; we will come no more unto thee? Can a maid forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? yet my people have forgotten me days without number.

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the challenge the accuser's reply to a false plea, recalls the long wicked reign in which prophets rebuked at the risk of their lives, notes that the pronoun stands in an unusual place, reads the land of darkness as literally a darkness of Jah with the divine name expressing intensity, renders the boast as we rove at will, and identifies the bride's article as the girdle that marked a wife.

Gill has them chiding as if God dealt hardly with them, reports the rabbinic reading of the smiting as for vanity, passes on the tradition that the pot of manna was brought out and shown, and describes the jewels that keep a bride from sleeping; Calvin notes that the verb of pleading takes a preposition of opposition, sets beside the wasted chastisement the older prophet's complaint, defends the command to see rather than hear, and asks whether anything among precious stones can compare with God.

Clarke asks whether any needful blessing was ever withheld, expands the boast into a manifesto of refusing all restraint human or divine, and dates the forgetting to the fifty-five years of one reign; Wesley makes the children the inhabitants of each city, turns correction into instruction, says they shall see because their ears are shut, and calls the boast words of pride.
Henry calls the denial the greatest absurdity, since the plea will be overruled and they know they have all transgressed alike.

debates.question: Why are they told to see rather than to hear?

positions.position: Because a thing was shown them, the pot of manna being brought out for their conviction.
Because they are asked not to be taught but to know, the appeal being to a fact they may see with their own eyes.
Because their ears are shut against it.
Because the pronoun is placed for emphasis: O generation, you, I mean, see ye.

debates.question: What did they mean by saying they were lords?

positions.position: Better rendered we rove at will: Israel claims the power to do as she likes.
A manifesto of independence: we will be our own masters, and regard no laws human or divine.
Words of pride and boasting.

debates.question: What is the force of the forgotten ornaments?

positions.position: Jewels laid by for a wedding day, never out of the mind, so that the bride can scarcely sleep for thinking of them.
An attachment greater than theirs to God, since women look back with pleasure in old age on the dress they wore in youth.
The girdle that marked a wife, treasured for life as a marriage ring is, so that the memorial is kept while the husband is forgotten.
A comparison of worth: girls value such trinkets more than life, and nothing among precious stones compares with God.

outliers.claim: Notes that the verb of pleading takes a preposition of opposition, so that the sense is, why should ye contend against me.
Recalls the long wicked reign in which prophets who rebuked did so at the risk of their lives and innocent blood was shed from one end of the city to the other.

themes: Wherefore will ye plead with me? ye all have transgressed against me, saith the Lord.
In vain have I smitten your children; they received no correction: your own sword hath devoured your prophets, like a destroying lion.
O generation, see ye the word of the Lord. Have I been a wilderness unto Israel? a land of darkness? wherefore say my people, We are lords; we will come no more unto thee?
Can a maid forget her ornaments, or a bride her attire? yet my people have forgotten me days without number.

33.pericope_label: Why trimmest thou thy way to seek love? therefore hast thou also taught the wicked ones thy ways. Also in thy skirts is found the blood of the souls of the poor innocents: I have not found it by secret search, but upon all these. Yet thou sayest, Because I am innocent, surely his anger shall turn from me. Behold, I will plead with thee, because thou sayest, I have not sinned. Why gaddest thou about so much to change thy way? thou also shalt be ashamed of Egypt, as thou wast ashamed of Assyria. Yea, thou shalt go forth from him, and thine hands upon thine head: for the Lord hath rejected thy confidences, and thou shalt not prosper in them.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch explain the confidence of the plea from a long peace and the non-fulfilment of older threats, make the gadding a running and the change of way a shift from Assyrian help to Egyptian, and read the going forth as a return from Egypt with the hands beaten on the head; Ellicott hears the trimming as scornful irony on the word men used for reform, lays out the alternatives in the obscure clause about searching, hears the accused take up the accuser's own word innocent, and catches the frequentative force of the gadding.

Gill takes the trimming cosmetically of a woman dressing to excite her lovers, allows either the sacrificed infants or the slain prophets for the blood, and reports the rival derivations of the word for gadding; Calvin says flatly that all the interpreters are mistaken about the blood, calls their profession of innocence a brazen front, and sets out the calculation of distances that made the Egyptian policy look sound.

Clarke reports a rendering that personifies calamity and instructs it where to find them, gives the alternative about a dug hole against blood sprinkled openly on consecrated oaks, and identifies the hand laid on the head as the sign of deep sorrow at utter desolation; Wesley reads the trimming as decking to entice help and calls the gesture the usual posture of mourning.

debates.question: What is the trimming of the way?

positions.position: A woman painting and dressing herself to excite her lovers, and labouring for a meretricious hire.
Scornful irony on the very word men used for reform: what is this amendment that leads only to further indulgence?
A rendering that personifies the punishment: therefore have I taught calamity thy ways.
Decking thyself, and so enticing others to thy help.

debates.question: How is the clause about not finding it by secret search to be read?

positions.position: Others cover blood so that it may not appear, but these shed it openly and sprinkled it on their consecrated oaks.
Either the blood was not found by a search such as men make who dig through a house wall, being patent everywhere, or else those killed had not been caught breaking in.

debates.question: Whose blood is in the skirts?

positions.position: Either the infants of the poor sacrificed to Moloch, or the prophets who were slain.
The children first, and perhaps also the maltreated prophets.
Not general cruelty at all, as every interpreter has supposed, but the raging of the people against the prophets sent to heal them.

outliers.claim: Sets out the calculation that made the Egyptian policy look sound, the enemy twenty or thirty days away and the helper able to come at the shortest warning, and says they were greatly mistaken.
Extends the sentence to both powers alike: as God broke the power of Assyria, so will he overthrow the might of Egypt, making all trust in it a shame.
